name: Pale Sage
lede: Pale Sage is a pale shade of [[sage|sage]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body: Pale Sage joins the modifier *pale* to the base color [[sage]], named for the herb's grey-green leaf [1][4]. It sits very high in lightness, 87 on the LCH scale, with chroma of only 9, so faint that Ridgway's own notation leaves it without a Munsell reading [1][4]. The ISCC-NBS system calls the matching block, 153, 'greenish white,' a Delta-E of 6.0 from this article's value [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[pale-niagara-green]] and [[grey-white]], at 3.3 and 4.2 ΔE [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 1.77% of 23,781 paintings, 421 paintings; within a single canvas it reads as a distinct area in 289 of them [3]. That ranks it more common than 76% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks earlier than most names, in the 1200s, found in 3.5% of that century's thin 142-painting record, 5 paintings, 2.2 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, by lightness rank, in 70% of its 289 appearances[3]. Paul Signac is its most devoted painter, using it in 5 of his 18 works here, 7.1 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [3]. The earliest dated appearance is a 1256 painting by Ma Lin, 656 years before the name's first documented record in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from the United Kingdom, 2.3 times the expected rate, 33 of 593 British paintings in our archive [3]. It shares canvases with [[charcoal-grey]] and [[leek-green]] more often than chance, lifts of 5.0 and 4.2 [3].
